statements.quote: The Department of Justice can put you in jail. I think that's highly unlikely
statements.context: The DOJ opened a non-public antitrust investigation into UnitedHealth Group in October 2023 and served a document preservation notice. The author notes the DOJ can jail people but judges jail highly unlikely; the trailing sentence implies antitrust enforcement, amid the Change Healthcare ransomware attack, is the more plausible outcome.
statements.note: Negative call (no jail for UHG executives). Sentence trails off into 'anti-trust enforcement... where the FBI could be of help in decrypting files'.

statements.quote: Change Healthcare may be down for a very long time.
statements.context: From a background conversation with a cybersecurity professional: average 73 days to resolve a ransomware attack, but BlackCat is an unreliable actor who may re-encrypt after a decrypt key is bought. Author forecasts the Change Healthcare outage could last a very long time.
statements.note: Outage-duration call; base rate of 73 days given as setup.

statements.quote: The market rate for a breach of the scale is around $40 million, which is not that much money for United Healthcare
statements.context: Author relays a cybersecurity source's estimate that the going ransom for a breach of this scale is about $40 million, small next to UHG's $8.9 billion quarterly earnings. Read as an implicit estimate of the ransom UHG would face.
statements.note: Borderline: phrased as a market rate, not an explicit prediction; sourced to an unnamed cybersecurity professional. Same $40M figure reused later as the ransom comparator.

statements.quote: The much bigger financial problem for United Healthcare is that the information in question is all protected health information, that, for an average of hundreds of days, was being accessed by somebody in a way that is a violation of HIPAA.
statements.context: Author argues the HIPAA exposure (protected health information accessed for hundreds of days) will be a far larger financial problem for UnitedHealth than the ransom payment itself.
statements.note: Restated later in the post as 'The cyber security issue is the least of United Healthcare's problems'.

statements.quote: If there is documentation that they knew before, the fines on the HIPAA breach and the scale of that HIPAA breach may be financially catastrophic in a way that a $40 million ransom payment would be trivial next to.
statements.context: UHG had 48 hours to report the breach to HHS. Conditional: if documents show UHG/Change knew of the intrusion earlier than reported, HIPAA fines may be financially catastrophic, dwarfing a $40 million ransom.
statements.note: Conditional call.

statements.quote: “What did they know and when did they know it” is going to be a really important question.
statements.context: Author forecasts that the timing of UnitedHealth's knowledge of the Change Healthcare intrusion will become a central question, feeding both HIPAA penalties and the DOJ records preservation request.

statements.quote: there may be some pissed-off for our cyber security professionals who have every incentive to report what they knew
statements.context: Optum laid off cybersecurity staff just before the breach was reported. Author expects some fired professionals may report what the company knew, linking to the DOJ preservation-of-records request.
statements.note: Whistleblower call; hedged.

statements.quote: And my guess is they were out of compliance with that cyber security standard.
statements.context: The preceding sentence says field security standards, which determine whether UHG's cyber insurance will cover the breach, require an 'air gap' backup. Author guesses UHG/Change were out of compliance, implying the insurance may not pay.
statements.note: Estimate of a past/present hidden fact (compliance at time of breach), not a future state; logged for the implied insurance-coverage consequence.

statements.quote: The cyber security issue is the least of United Healthcare's problems, it's the HIPAA breach on top of the cyber security invasion that causes a compliance nightmare
statements.context: Author says the HIPAA breach, layered on the cyber intrusion, will create a compliance nightmare for UnitedHealth that outweighs the cybersecurity problem itself; he then walks through per-record HIPAA penalty tiers.
statements.note: Restatement of the earlier 'much bigger financial problem' call in the same post.

statements.quote: So we're talking about a worst-case scenario of $1.8×10^14.
statements.context: Tier-4 HIPAA penalty math: $1.8 million maximum per record times about 100 million people (Change Healthcare processes data on 1/3 of Americans) gives $1.8×10^14, which the author says is 377 times UnitedHealth's market capitalization. He labels it explicitly a worst-case scenario.
statements.note: Explicit upper bound, not a stated expectation ('That's a worst-case scenario.'); logged for recall.

statements.quote: All of us should care. And will, in the coming days.
statements.context: On the Change Healthcare outage's effects on providers and patients (not getting paid, not getting meds), the author predicts everyone will come to care in the coming days.
statements.note: 'should care' is normative but 'And will' carries a predictive reading.

statements.quote: there is likely to have been a data breach although that has not been confirmed by Change Healthcare at this stage
statements.context: Quoted from HIPAA Journal: BlackCat uses double extortion (exfiltrate, then encrypt), so a data breach is likely though unconfirmed by Change Healthcare. The author introduces it as evidence the problem is 'getting more grim by the day' and later treats the HIPAA breach as fact.
statements.note: Quoted third party (HIPAA Journal); author adopts it ('millions of patient records at risk', 'the HIPAA breach'). Forward-looking reading: a data breach will be confirmed.

statements.quote: Today's The Frontier Psychiatrist post is an imagined meeting where the BlackCat cyber hackers discuss why they haven't gotten paid from United Healthcare, yet.
statements.context: Author's own (non-satirical) intro to the BlackCat town-hall satire. The word 'yet' implies he expects UnitedHealth to eventually pay BlackCat's ransom for the Change Healthcare attack.
statements.note: Implicit forecast carried by 'yet'; borderline.

statements.quote: we are optimistic, we are on a second-level appeal, and we're confident we're going to get the ransom we requested
statements.context: Spoken by the fictional BlackCat spokesperson in the satirical all-hands, after jokes about UnitedHealth's fax-only ransom process and peer-to-peer appeals. Underlying claim: UnitedHealth will pay the ransom. Restated as 'we're hopeful that we're going to make a lot of money on this extortion'.
statements.note: Satirical voice of BlackCat; 'confident' is the character's. Underlying expectation (UHG pays) matches the author's own 'yet' in the intro; coder may flip sincere.

statements.quote: And if placebo response is getting more and more robust (according to expert raters), that becomes harder.
statements.context: Citing a meta-analysis (Rief et al. 2009) showing rising expert-rated placebo response in antidepressant trials, the author says beating placebo to demonstrate efficacy becomes harder if that trend continues.
statements.note: Conditional trend statement; borderline forward-looking (trend continuation makes trials harder).

statements.quote: We should expect a storm of these reviews, meta-reviews, and network-meta-meta-meta analyses.
statements.context: After critiquing the Yao et al. 2024 psychedelic meta-analysis (Psychiatry Research) for omitting the MindMed MM-120 LSD trial, the author predicts a flood of reviews and meta-analyses on psychedelic medicine because they are easier than original research; adds 'even not-so-good reviews will get cited'.
statements.note: 'should expect' is predictive, not normative.

statements.quote: Except, in this case, that means…just closing those things as they currently stand
statements.context: Author's reading of UnitedHealth's statement to Endpoints News about 'continually reviewing capabilities': Optum's virtual care business will be closed as it currently stands. The post title recalls his earlier call that 'Optum Virtual Care' might be shutting down; he writes 'I was right'.
statements.note: Restatement/confirmation of the author's earlier shutdown call; shutdown reported as planned, with July last dates per Endpoints.

statements.quote: Employees in the virtual care unit were notified about the plan to shut down the business during an April 18 conference call with Optum Everycare CEO Jennifer Phalen, according to three people with direct knowledge of the call. Some employees were told that their last date will be in July, the people said.
statements.context: Endpoints News report quoted by the author: Optum's virtual care unit is to shut down; some employees' last day is in July 2024.
statements.note: Third-party reporting quoted by the author, who presents it as confirmation of his own earlier call.

statements.quote: Oh my. They can always acquire more.
statements.context: Quip after the Optum Virtual Care shutdown and layoff news; implies Optum/UnitedHealth will keep acquiring companies.
statements.note: Cynical aside; borderline as a forecast (continued acquisitions).

statements.quote: Look, the future is AI. And in the future, I don’t have to any more notes.
statements.context: Line spoken by 'Owen Moore, MD', the author's alter ego, in his fictional TV pilot set one week before the Covid pandemic (2020), after revealing a HIPAA-compliant ceiling microphone array. Underlying claim: AI will take over clinical note-writing. The author elsewhere describes building 'AI-guided healthcare'.
statements.note: Fictional frame with ironic disclaimer; the foil line 'That's never happening' (character Allegra) is not the author's view. Coder may flip sincere.
